title: Acyltransferase inhibitors: a patent review (2010-present).
text_summary: 本研究综述了2010年至目前发表的专利，其中涉及ACAT、DGAT和MGAT等酰基转移酶的异构酶选择性抑制剂，这些酶与中性脂质代谢有关。研究发现，ACAT、DGAT和MGAT的异构酶在人体中性脂质代谢中发挥不同的功能，并被考虑为潜在的治疗靶点。因此，研究人员寻找可用于治疗或预防脂质代谢紊乱的异构酶选择性抑制剂。其中，吡吡罗酚A衍生物、ACAT2选择性抑制剂可能成为治疗动脉粥样硬化、纯合子家族性高胆固醇血症和非酒精性脂肪性肝病的潜在药物。此外，研究还发现，PPPA衍生物在体内具有口服活性，可降低动脉粥样硬化小鼠模型中的血浆胆固醇水平和动脉粥样硬化病变，同时不会引起副作用。这些发现促进了研究人员寻找更有效、更选择性的PPPA衍生物。总之，本研究表明，酰基转移酶异构酶选择性抑制剂在治疗脂质代谢紊乱方面具有巨大的潜力。

Acyltransferase inhibitors: a
patent review (2010--present)
Taichi Ohshiro & Hiroshi Tomoda†
†Kitasato University, Graduate School of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Tokyo, Japan
Introduction: Acyltransferase (AT) catalyzes the transfer of an acyl moiety
from acyl-coenzyme A (acyl-CoA) to an acceptor. ATs play important roles in
the maintenance of homeostasis in the human body and have been linked
to various diseases; therefore, several ATs have been proposed as potential
targets for the treatment or prevention of such diseases. The AT family
includes acyl-CoA:cholesterol AT (ACAT), diacylglycerol AT (DGAT), and mono-
acylglycerol AT (MGAT) for the metabolism of lipids. Furthermore, recent
molecular biological studies revealed the existence of their isozymes with
distinct functions in the body.
Areas covered: This review summarized patent filings published between
2010 and the present date that claimed isozyme-selective inhibitors of ACAT,
DGAT and MGAT, which are involved in neutral lipid metabolism.
Expert opinion: Isozymes of ACAT, DGAT and MGAT play distinct functions in
neutral lipid metabolism in the human body and have been considered as poten-
tial therapeutic targets. Accordingly, isozyme-selective inhibitors that could be
used in the treatment or prevention of lipid metabolism disorders were searched
for. Of these, pyripyropene A derivatives, ACAT2-selective inhibitors, may be
potential therapeutics for the treatment of atherosclerosis, homozygous familial
hypercholesterolemia and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.
Keywords: acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferase, diacylglycerol acyltransferase, inhibitor,
isozyme, monoacylglycerol acyltransferase, neutral lipid metabolism
Expert Opin. Ther. Patents [Early Online]
1. Introduction
Acyltransferase (AT) catalyzes the transfer of an acyl group from a substrate such as
acyl-coenzyme A (acyl-CoA) to an acceptor in most cases and plays important roles
in the human body. Over 200 AT enzymes have been identified in the database
to date.
One of the recent topics examined in relation to ATs is ghrelin O-AT (GOAT,
EC 2.3.1). Ghrelin is a 28 amino acid peptide hormone mainly produced by stom-
ach tissue [1,2]. GOAT, also known as membrane-bound O-AT domain-containing
protein 4, catalyzes the transfer of an octanoyl residue from n-octanoyl-CoA to the
Ser-3 position of the peptide ghrelin. This unique acyl modification is crucial for
the physiological functions of ghrelin, including those associated with food intake,
obesity and the secretion of insulin [3]. Therefore, GOAT has been considered as
a potential therapeutic target for the modulation of body weight gain and glucose
control [4]. In WO2010/039461, a GOAT inhibitor (GO-CoA-Tat, Figure 1) was
filed as a potential therapeutic agent for obesity and type 2 diabetes. Barnett et al.
reported that GO-CoA-Tat (40 mg/kg/day, i.p. 1 month) improved glucose toler-
ance and reduced weight gain in wild type mice, but not in ghrelin-knockout
mice [5].
In the field of lipid metabolism, over 10 AT enzymes are involved in the biosyn-
thesis of triacylglycerol (TG), cholesteryl ester (CE) and phospholipids. Particularly,
neutral lipids TG and CE are regarded to be closely linked to dyslipidemia, and ATs

potential targets for the treatment of dyslipidemia. This
review focuses on the three ATs; acyl-CoA:cholesterol AT
(ACAT, also known as sterol O-AT), diacylglycerol AT
(DGAT), and monoacylglycerol AT (MGAT). Recent molec-
ular biological studies demonstrated that these ATs had iso-
zymes with distinct functions, which led to attempts to
identify isozyme-selective inhibitors. The number of patents
in which the inhibitors of these ATs were filed is summarized
in Table 1, and showed that, in the past 5 years, DGAT has
become the most attractive therapeutic target.
Statins, well-known inhibitors of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglu-
taryl coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, which is a rate-
limiting enzyme of cholesterol biosynthesis, have been used
clinically to treat hypercholesterolemia and atherosclerosis,
and have retained the top position in the world sale ranking
of medical drugs for many years [6]. However, clinical data
showed that even in patients treated with statins, the risk of
complications and death from cardiovascular (CV) events
was only reduced by 30%
[7]. The US FDA recently
announced an increased risk of muscle injury (myopathy
and rhabdomyolysis) in patients treated with high doses of
statins [8,9]. Ezetimibe, an inhibitor of a cholesterol transporter
(Niemann-Pick C1 Like 1 protein), was launched in 2006 as a
new type of cholesterol-lowering drug [10]. However, the
ENHANCE trial demonstrated that combined therapy with
ezetimibe and simvastatin did not lead to significant changes
in the progression of atherosclerosis over that with simvastatin
only therapy in patients with heterozygous familial hypercho-
lesterolemia (FH) [11]. Therefore, the quest for novel pharma-
cological agents that target selective steps in lipid metabolism
has intensified significantly in recent years.
Since interest in preventive medicines for health care has
increased, particularly in developed countries, research on
post-statin drug discovery has begun to focus on the
accumulation of neutral lipids in the human body. The three
ATs involved in neutral lipid metabolism, ACAT, DGAT and
MGAT, are responsible for the synthesis of TG or CE in the
body. The excessive accumulation of TG and/or CE due to a
fat-rich
diet
or
sedentary
lifestyle
causes
obesity,
type 2 diabetes, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)
and atherosclerosis. These ATs are known to have isozymes
with distinct functions; therefore, research has focused on
the identification of isozyme-selective inhibitors.

and

future prospects of these inhibitors have also been discussed
as an expert opinion.
2. ACAT isozymes and inhibitors
The enzyme ACAT (EC 2.3.1.26), which catalyzes the syn-
thesis of CE from free cholesterol and long-chain fatty acyl-
CoA, is considered to be a promising therapeutic target [12].
ACAT plays important roles in mammals; it aids the absorp-
tion of dietary cholesterol from the intestines, the production
of very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) in the liver, and the
formation of foam cells from macrophages in the arterial
wall. Therefore, inhibiting the activity of ACAT is expected
not only to lower plasma cholesterol levels, but also to have
a direct effect on the arterial wall. The interest of many phar-
maceutical companies in ACAT as a promising target enzyme
for the development of novel anti-atherosclerotic agents has
markedly increased in recent years. Accordingly, a large num-
ber of synthetic ACAT inhibitors, containing ureas, imida-
zoles and amide moieties, have been reported in patents and
studies [12]. However, no inhibitors have been clinically used
to date, and the number of patents filed on ACAT inhibitors
has markedly decreased (Table 1).
Two ACAT isozymes, ACAT1 and ACAT2, have been
identified in various mammals. Chang’s group succeeded in
cloning a cDNA for the first ACAT gene (Acat1) from human
monocytes [13]. The second ACAT gene (Acat2) was then
cloned from the liver and intestine by three different
groups [14-16]. The human ACAT1 gene encodes a 550 amino
acid protein, while the human ACAT2 gene encodes proteins
of 522 amino acids. Human ACAT2 is ~ 40% identical to
human ACAT1. Both ACAT isozymes are membrane pro-
teins localized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and are
assumed to possess several hydrophobic domains that can
penetrate the ER membrane [17,18].
Since the discovery of the ACAT1 and ACAT2 isozymes,
the findings of extensive genetic studies including knockout
mice have indicated that these isozymes have distinct func-
tions. ACAT1 is ubiquitously expressed in the sebaceous
glands,
steroidogenic
tissues
and
macrophages,
while
ACAT2 is selectively expressed in the liver and intestine [19].
Controversy has existed over which isozyme is predominant
in the human liver (hepatocytes and Kupffer cells). However,

Rudel’s group demonstrated using human liver biopsy sam-
ples and an ACAT2-selective inhibitor (pyripyropene A
[PPPA]) that ACAT2 was expressed as the dominant ACAT
isozyme in hepatocytes, whereas ACAT1 was only expressed
in Kupffer cells [20]. ACAT1-knockout mice (Acat1-/- mice)
were created by two different groups in order to elucidate
the roles of the ACAT1 isozyme [21-23]. ACAT1-deficient
(Acat1-/-) mice were found to be viable and fertile, and
ACAT activity was detected in the liver and intestines, but
was completely absent in the adrenal cortex and peritoneal
macrophages. However, in addition to dry eye syndrome,
Acat1-/- mice lacked apolipoprotein E or the LDL receptor,
similar to atherogenic mouse models, were susceptible to ath-
erosclerosis, and had extensive cutaneous xanthomatosis with
the loss of hair [21]. Free cholesterol content was significantly
increased in their skin. In contrast, ACAT activity was
completely absent in the liver and intestines of ACAT2-defi-
cient (Acat2-/-) mice, and these mice were completely resistant
to diet-induced hypercholesterolemia, the formation of cho-
lesterol gallstones and atherosclerosis [24,25]. Rudel’s group
also reported that hepatic steatosis (NAFLD) was prevented
in liver-specific ACAT2 antisense oligonucleotide-treated
mice and Acat2-/- mice due to enhancements in the mobiliza-
tion of hepatic TG [26,27]. These findings on ACAT isozymes
strongly suggested the importance of ACAT isozyme-selective
inhibitors as potential therapeutics.
A number of microbial and synthetic ACAT inhibitors
have been published and filed in patents and studies [12].
However, data on the selectivity of these inhibitors toward
ACAT isozymes was absent before 2003. Researchers began
to show the selectivity of ACAT inhibitors to these isozymes
after 2003. Accordingly, avasimibe [28] and pactimibe (Fig-
ure 2) [29] were reported to be dual inhibitors; they moderately
inhibited both ACAT1 and ACAT2. Unfortunately, attempts
to use these inhibitors clinically were unsuccessful [30-32].
Nissen et al. reported that clinical treatments with pactimibe
did not slow the progression of atherosclerosis, and even pro-
moted atherosclerosis [31]. Fazio and Linton suggested that the
inhibition of ACAT1 by pactimibe had toxic effects on mac-
rophages and vascular cells due to the excessive accumulation
of free cholesterol because these cells did not have cholesterol
efflux systems [33].
K-604 (Figure 2) [28], an ACAT1-selective inhibitor that
was recently filed by Kowa, also failed to reduce atherosclero-
sis and CV events in clinical trials. In WO2011/161964,
Kowa researchers showed that K-604 improved glucose toler-
ance and reduced blood glucose levels in in vivo experiments
using LDL receptor-knockout (Ldlr-/-) mice and WHHL rab-
bits. The treatment of Ldlr-/- mice with K-604 at 0.3 and
3 mg/kg/day and pactimibe at 0.1 mg/kg/day lowered glucose
and insulin levels in the plasma and improved homeostasis
model assessment ratio (HOMA-R; plasma insulin (µU/ml)
 plasma glucose (mg/dl)/405), an indicator of insulin resis-
tance, after a 1-week treatment. Furthermore, WHHL rabbits
treated with K-604 (20 and 40 mg/kg/day) for 12 weeks had
decreased insulin plasma levels and improved HOMA-R.
This patent indicated that K-604 improved insulin resistance.
As one of the mechanisms responsible, one research group
reported that insulin promoted expression of the ACAT1
gene via MAPK and CCAT/enhancer binding protein in vitro
[34]. However, the in vivo mechanism involved between
ACAT1 and insulin resistance (or type 2 diabetes) currently
remains unclear.
Among microbial ACAT inhibitors, PPPA (Figure 2), origi-
nally identified as a potent ACAT inhibitor that was isolated
from a culture broth of Aspergillus fumigatus FO-1289 by
researchers at the Kitasato Institute and Kitasato University in
1993 [35-37], was shown to selectively and strongly inhibit the
activity of the ACAT2 isozyme [38-40]. Furthermore, Das et al.
reported that PPPA is noncovalently bound to the specific site
(Gln492--Val493--Ser494ofthe5th transmembranedomain [18])
of ACAT2 isozymes [41]. Of the natural pyripyropenes [35-37] and
semisynthetic derivatives [42-46] reported (filed in JP 8-259569, JP
8-291164, JP 8-269062, JP 8-269063, JP 8-269064, JP
8-269065 and JP 8-269066), PPPA showed the highest selectiv-
ity toward theACAT2 isozyme [47]. Therefore, thein vivo efficacy
of the ACAT2-selective inhibitor was tested for the first time.
PPPA was found to be orally active in vivo, and reduced plasma
cholesterol levels and atherosclerotic lesions in atherogenic mouse
models without causing side effects [48]. Furthermore, the accu-
mulation of neutral lipids, mainly CE levels in the liver, was
decreased in PPPA-treated mice. These findings promoted
researchers at Kitasato University to search for more potent and
ACAT2-selective PPPA derivatives. The in vitro metabolism of
PPPA in plasma and liver microsomes in various animal samples
was consequently investigated [49]. In liver microsomes collected
from humans, rabbits, rats and mice, successive hydrolysis
occurred at the 1-O-acetyl residue, then at the 11-O-acetyl resi-
due of PPPA, while the 7-O-acetyl residue was resistant to
hydrolysis (Figure 3A). On the other hand, hydrolysis of the
7-O-acetyl
residue
only

in

(Figure 3A). All the PPPA metabolites observed in liver micro-
somes and plasma markedly decreased ACAT2 inhibitory activ-
ity. These findings indicated that the three O-acetyl residues of
PPPA were essential for inhibitory activity toward the
ACAT2 isozyme. Second-generation PPPA derivatives were
then semisynthetically prepared

fat absorption in the intestine, and the assembly of lipoprotein
particles (VLDL and chylomicron) from the liver and

intestines [53]. The excessive accumulation of TG due to a fat-
rich diet or sedentary lifestyle is associated with various dis-
eases such as obesity, NAFLD, type 2 diabetes and hypertrigly-
ceridemia. Therefore, inhibitors of TG biosynthesis can
protect patients against obesity and other disorders
[54].
DGAT (acyl-CoA:1,2-diacyl-sn-glycerol O-AT, EC 2.3.1.20)
is a membrane-bound enzyme that catalyzes the reaction
involving the transfer of an acyl residue from acyl-CoA to diac-
ylglycerol (DG) to form TG [55,56]. This reaction is the final
step of de novo TG biosynthesis in both the monoacylglycerol
(MG) and glycerol phosphate pathways. However, the DGAT
enzyme has not yet been purified because it is a hydrophobic
transmembrane protein in the ER.
Two DGAT isozymes have been identified in mammals:
DGAT1 and DGAT2 [16,57,58]. Farese’s groups identified the
first gene encoding a mammalian DGAT (Dgat1) from its
homology to ACAT genes [57]. The full-length cDNA of
mouse DGAT1 encodes a 498 amino acid protein that
is ~ 20% identical to mouse ACAT1, with the most highly
conserved region existing in the C-terminus. Its mRNA has
been detected in every mammalian tissue, and the highest
expression levels have been observed in the adipose tissue
and small intestine. These findings are consistent with the
proposed role of DGAT in the intestinal absorption of dietary
fat. However, its mRNA expression was found to be relatively
low in the livers of humans despite high DGAT activity, sug-
gesting the existence of a second DGAT in the liver. Accord-
ingly, the second DGAT gene (Dgat2) was identified by
mammalian
homologs
and
also
by
a
fungal
DGAT
enzyme
[58]. DGAT2 showed no homology with the
DGAT1 isozyme, but showed homology with MGAT. The
protein with 387 amino acids in humans has one or two pos-
sible transmembrane domain(s). Its mRNA has also been
detected in every mammalian tissue with high expression lev-
els in adipose tissue and the liver.
Since the discovery of DGAT isozymes, the findings of
extensive genetic studies, including those involving knockout
mice, have provided novel insights into DGAT. Newborn
DGAT2-knockout (Dgat2-/-) mice die soon after birth [59].
TG contents in the carcasses were markedly reduced
by ~ 90%, and these mice lacked the substrates for oxidative
metabolism. Essential fatty acids were also absent, resulting
in abnormalities in skin lipid and epidermal barrier functions.
Therefore, newborn Dgat2-/- mice rapidly became dehydrated,
which hastened their demise. On the other hand, DGAT1-
knockout (Dgat1-/-) mice were found to be viable and had
more modest reductions in tissue TG content [60]. The adi-
pose mass of adult Dgat1-/- mice was ~ 50% less than that
of wild-type mice on a chow diet and their adipocytes were
also smaller [60,61]. Although tissue TG levels were decreased
in these mice, DG and free fatty acid (FFA) levels were not
significantly elevated, while plasma TG levels were normal.
These findings indicated that DGAT2 played an essential
role in TG metabolism, whereas that of DGAT1 was limited.
Previous studies on DGAT-deficient mice reported that
pharmacological interventions using DGAT1 may represent
a
useful
strategy
for
the
treatment
of
obesity
and
type 2 diabetes, whereas the inhibition of DGAT2 as an
anti-obesity therapy may face the obstacle of a narrow thera-
peutic window. Therefore, a large number of DGAT isozyme
inhibitors have been published as patents (Table 1).
Microbial and synthetic DGAT inhibitors had been pub-
lished in a patent prior to the discovery of DGAT isozymes [62].
For example, amidepsines (JP 8-182496) and roselipins
(WO99/41265) were isolated from the fungal culture broths
of Humicola spp. FO-2942 [63,64] and FO-5969 [65] and Gliocla-
dium roseum KF-1040 [66,67], respectively. Most of these fungal
compounds moderately inhibited DGAT with IC50 values of
between 10 and 20 µM in enzyme assays using rat liver micro-
somes [62]. On the other hand, some synthetic DGAT inhibitors
potently inhibited DGAT with nanomolar IC50 values.
DGAT2 inhibitors have rarely been published. For example,
roselipins [68] and synthetic imidazo[4, 5-b]pyridine derivatives
(WO2013/150416 invented by Pfizer, Inc.) were reported to
inhibit the DGAT2 isozyme (Figure 4). Derivatives 1 and 2
gave IC50 values of 13.8 and 14.5 nM, respectively, in an
enzyme assay using a membrane fraction prepared from human
DGAT2-expressing Sf-9 cells. However, none of the patents
including those on 1 and 2, except for roselipins [68], showed
DGAT1 inhibitory activities or SI value toward DGAT1 and
2 (e.g., roselipin 1A, IC50 for DGAT1 vs IC50 for
DGAT2: > 200 µM vs 30 µM).
As shown in Table 1, the number of patents filed on
DGAT1 inhibitors has become larger than those on other AT
inhibitors [62,69-71]. Representative synthetic DGAT1 inhibitors
are shown in Figure 5. Following the discovery of DGAT iso-
zymes, a number of DGAT1 inhibitors, for example, LCQ908,
T863, PF-04620110, BAY744113, urea-based derivative 3,
AZD3988 and pyridine-amide derivative 4, were identified as
first-generation derivatives [70,71]. These generally have a terminal
carboxylicacidresidueand/orheterocyclicringintheirstructures.
LCQ908, which was developed by Novartis, is currently under-
going Phase III trials for the treatment of familial chylomicrone-
mia syndrome; however, the findings have not yet been reported.
Several pharmaceutical companies have developed second-
generation DGAT1 inhibitors and published their findings.
In WO2011/031628, WO2012/024179, WO2012/112364,
WO2012/122075, WO2013/096093 and WO2013/130370
(invented by Merck and Schering groups), pyridine-carboximide
derivatives 5 and 6, ractam derivatives 7 and 8, and azole deriva-
tives 9 and 10 were filed as DGAT1 inhibitors (Figure 5). In
WO2010/070343, WO2010/146395 and WO2011/121350
(invented by AstraZeneca UK Ltd.), 1, 3, 4-oxadiazole deriva-
tive 11, pyrazine carboxamide derivative 12 and ractam deriva-
tive 13 were filed as DGAT1 inhibitors. Benzamide derivative
14 in WO2011/071840 (invented by Eli Lilly), ractam deriva-
tives 15 and 16, pyrazolo[1, 5-a]pyrimidine derivatives 17
and 18, and urea-based derivative 19 in WO2012/162129,
WO2014/081994, WO2014/081995 and WO2014/081996
(invented by GlaxoSmithKline) were also filed as DGAT1

4. MGAT isozymes and inhibitors
MGAT (EC 2.3.1.22) is a membrane-bound enzyme that cat-
alyzes the transfer of acyl residue from acyl-CoA to MG to
form DG [56]. This reaction is the first step in the MG path-
way of de novo TG biosynthesis. MGAT plays an important
role in the absorption of dietary fat in the intestine, in which
dietary TG is digested, and the resulting MG and FFAs are
reused to produce TG in enterocytes. Resynthesized TG is
crucial for the assembly and secretion of chylomicrons.
The MGAT enzyme has not yet been purified because it is
a hydrophobic transmembrane protein in the ER. However,
three MGAT isozymes, MGAT1, MGAT2 and MGAT3,
have been identified. In 2002, Farese’s group succeeded in
cloning the cDNA for the first MGAT gene (Mgat1) from a
mouse [72]. In 2003, the second MGAT gene (Mgat2) was
cloned from the mouse small intestine by two different
groups [73,74]. The third MGAT gene (Mgat3) was cloned
from the human small intestine
[75]. The MGAT1 gene
(mouse) encodes a 335 amino acid protein, the MGAT2
gene (mouse) has 334 amino acids and the MGAT3 gene
(human) has 341 amino acids [72-75]. All MGAT isozymes
were
found
to
have
high
homology
with
DGAT2.
A previous study showed that MGAT1 was mainly expressed
in
the
stomach,
kidney
and
adipose
tissue,
whereas
MGAT2 and MGAT3 were highly expressed in the small
intestine [76]. Furthermore, MGAT3 has only been detected
in higher mammals and humans, and not in rodents [75,77].
Since the discovery of MGAT isozymes, the findings of
extensive genetic studies, including knockout mice, have pro-
vided novel insights into MGAT. Most research groups have
focused on the MGAT2 isozyme, which is exclusively
expressed in the small intestine, because the MGAT pathway
accounts for ~ 75% of TG synthesis in the small intes-
tine [78,79] and MGAT2 plays a crucial role in the absorption
of dietary fat [80]. The MGAT2-knockout (Mgat2-/-) mice
prepared by Farese’s group were viable, fertile and healthy.
They had a normal phenotype (including weight gain and
body composition) on a low-fat diet similar to wild type
mice. On the other hand, on a high-fat diet, these Mgat2-/-
mice were protected against obesity, glucose tolerance, hyper-
cholesterolemia and NAFLD [80]. Moreover, energy expendi-
ture by intestine-specific Mgat2-/- mice was increased [81,82].
These knockout mouse experiments indicated that MGAT2
may be a potential target for the treatment of obesity and
metabolic diseases associated with excess caloric intake.

fied, the number of patents claiming MGAT inhibitors is still
small (Table 1). Although derivatives were filed in five patents
as MGAT2 inhibitors, their inhibitory activities against
MGAT1 or MGAT3 were not shown. In WO2010/095767
(invented by Banyu Pharmaceutical Co. Ltd.), pyrimidine-4
(3H)-one derivatives (Figure 6) were filed as MGAT2 inhibitors.

5. Expert opinion
Statins, HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, have been clinically
used as the gold standard treatment for hypercholesterolemia
and atherosclerosis over the past 20 years [6]. However, clinical
data have revealed several problems with their use: i) they only
reduce the risk of complications and related death from CV
events by 30% [7]; ii) they cause the serious adverse side effect
of muscle injury (myopathy and rhabdomyolysis) [8,9]; and
iii) they show none or low efficacy against homozygous
FH [83]. Ezetimibe, a cholesterol transporter inhibitor, was
recently launched as a new type of a cholesterol-lowering
drug in 2006 [10]. Unfortunately, the ENHANCE trial dem-
onstrated that the clinical efficacy of ezetimibe was low.
Therefore, new drugs with mechanisms of action that differ
from those of statins and ezetimibe are required for the treat-
ment of hypercholesterolemia and atherosclerosis [84].
In post-statin drug discovery, three ATs, ACAT, DGAT
and MGAT, have been considered as potential and promising
targets. Recent scientific advances revealed that these ATs had
isozymes with distinct functions in the body. Extensive studies
on the functions of each isozyme linked these ATs not only to
hypercholesterolemia and atherosclerosis but also to various
other disorders such as obesity, NAFLD and type 2 diabetes.
Therefore, the search for isozyme-selective inhibitors of
ACAT, DGAT or MGAT as post-statin drugs has intensified.
Unfortunately, these ATs, however, have not been purified so
far, and there are short of information about the three-
dimensional structures of ATs. Accordingly, it is difficult to
exert computer-based drug design or in silico drug screening.
Therefore, it will be the best way for researchers to discover
AT isozyme-selective inhibitors and to carry out ligand-based
drug design.
Two ACAT isozymes have been identified: ACAT1 and
ACAT2 [13-16]. In the 2000s, three synthetic ACAT inhibi-
tors, avasimibe [30], pactimibe [31,32] and K-604, failed in
clinical trials. Avasimibe and pactimibe inhibited both
ACAT1
and
ACAT2
(dual
type
inhibitors),
while
K-604 selectively inhibited ACAT1 [28,29]. Studies using
Acat1-/- mice showed that ACAT1-selective inhibition had
detrimental effects on atherosclerotic lesions, the skin and
eyes [21,23]. Furthermore, the inhibition of ACAT1 by dual
type or ACAT1-selective inhibitors were suggested to have
cytotoxic effects on macrophages and vascular cells in
humans due to the accumulation of cellular-free cholesterol,
which led to the worsening of atherosclerosis in clinical tri-
als [33]. A previous study using Acat2-/- mice showed that
ACAT2-selective inhibition had atheroprotective effects [25].
Accordingly, the ACAT2 isozyme represents a promising target
for the treatment of atherosclerosis. Fungal PPPA, the first
ACAT2-selective inhibitor, selectively inhibited hepatic and
intestinal ACAT2 activity and exhibited in vivo efficacy in

PPPA in atherogenic mouse and rabbit models. Furthermore,
ACAT2-selective inhibitors are expected to influence not only
atherosclerosis and hypercholesterolemia, including FH, but
also NAFLD [27]. Thus, the PPPA derivatives will be the
most promising candidates to be evaluated in clinical trials for
the post-statin drug development.
DGAT has two isozymes: DGAT1 and DGAT2 [16,57,58].
The results of knockout mouse experiments suggested that
DGAT1 may be a potential and safe target for the treatment
of obesity and type 2 diabetes, while DGAT2 may be a target
for an anti-obesity therapy, but faces the obstacle of a narrow
therapeutic window [62]. Accordingly, a number of DGAT1
inhibitors have been reported. Among them, development of
LCQ908 is most advanced in clinical trials (Phase III) [70].
As shown in Figure 5, however, other DGAT1 inhibitors
(Figure 5) have a similar structural skeleton (a terminal carbox-
ylic acid residue and heterocyclic ring). Therefore, DGAT1-
selective inhibitors with a distinct core structure are needed
as a next pipeline for drug development.
Three MGAT isozymes have so far been identified [72-75].
The MGAT2 isozyme is considered to be a potential target
for the treatment of obesity and metabolic diseases associated
with excess caloric intake, and several MGAT2 inhibitors
(Figure 6) have been reported. However, the crucial functions
of the MGAT isozymes remain unknown. Therefore, the
in vivo studies and the screening for MGAT1 and MGAT3-
slective inhibitors are still needed.
Thus, recent advance in the structural biology and knock-
out and/or transgenic mouse studies of ATs will accelerate
searching for novel AT isozyme-selective inhibitors. In the
near future, isozyme-selective inhibitors of ATs would be
launched as useful post-statin drugs.
